title: Democritus and the uncuttable bit
text: Around 400 BC, Democritus figured that if you keep cutting matter in half, you eventually hit pieces that can't be cut. He called them atoms, meaning uncuttable.
author: Democritus
source: Known through later ancient writers (c. 5th to 4th century BC); Wikipedia: Democritus
more:
Democritus lived roughly from 460 to 370 BC and built on ideas from the earlier thinker Leucippus. None of his own books survive. We know his views from later writers who quoted him or argued with him.

He had no way to test any of it. It was pure reasoning, and for about two thousand years it stayed that way. This thread follows how the guess finally got real evidence.

thread.title: How do we know atoms are real? (7 cards)

title: Dalton's whole-number clue
text: John Dalton noticed in the early 1800s that carbon and oxygen form two gases. For the same carbon, one has exactly twice the oxygen. Never 1.37 times.
source: Dalton, A New System of Chemical Philosophy (1808); Wikipedia: John Dalton, Law of multiple proportions
more:
The two gases are carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide. Dalton's explanation was that each element is made of identical atoms with their own weight, and compounds form when whole atoms join. You can't add half an atom, so the ratios jump in whole steps. His New System of Chemical Philosophy (1808) had the first table of relative atomic weights.

Plenty of scientists still treated atoms as handy bookkeeping. Nobody had seen one. The next clue came from a botanist's microscope.

thread.title: How do we know atoms are real? (7 cards)

title: Pollen that wouldn't sit still
text: In 1827, Robert Brown saw tiny particles from pollen grains jitter nonstop in water. Specks of glass did it too. So did rock dust.
source: Wikipedia: Brownian motion
more:
Brown was careful. The obvious guess was some life force in the pollen, so he tried particles that had never been alive. They danced the same way, which ruled out biology.

For decades nobody could explain it. People blamed heat currents, vibration or evaporation, but the jiggling never ran down, however still things were kept. The answer came in 1905, and it settled an argument that had lasted since Democritus.

thread.title: How do we know atoms are real? (7 cards)

title: Einstein predicts, Perrin measures
text: Einstein explained the jiggle in 1905: countless water molecules hitting each particle. He predicted how far it should drift. Jean Perrin measured it in 1908. It matched.
source: Wikipedia: Brownian motion; Nobel Prize in Physics 1926
more:
One molecule is far too small to budge a visible grain. But huge numbers of them hitting from all sides, a little unevenly from moment to moment, add up to a random walk. Einstein's formula tied the size of that wandering to how many molecules a given amount of substance contains.

Perrin's careful experiments with tiny grains won over most of the remaining sceptics. He got the 1926 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on the discontinuous structure of matter.

thread.title: How do we know atoms are real? (7 cards)

title: Shells bouncing off tissue paper
text: Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden fired alpha particles at thin metal foil in 1909. Most went straight through. About 1 in 8,000 bounced back.
source: Wikipedia: Rutherford scattering experiments; Atomic nucleus
more:
Rutherford later compared it to an artillery shell rebounding off tissue paper. In 1911 he worked out why. If an atom's charge and mass were spread evenly, as the leading model said, nothing should bounce back. Only a tiny, dense, positive core could do that.

That core, the nucleus, is tiny. Depending on the element, an atom is roughly 27,000 to 60,000 times wider than its nucleus. If the nucleus were a pea, the atom would be a few hundred metres across.

thread.title: How do we know atoms are real? (7 cards)

title: Why can't you walk through walls?
text: Atoms are almost entirely empty space. So when your hand hits a table, why does it stop instead of passing through like two clouds of gnats?
source: Wikipedia: Pauli exclusion principle
more:
Electrons, and a quantum rule about where they can be. The outer parts of atoms are clouds of negatively charged electrons, and those clouds push each other away when atoms get close. What you feel as touch is that push.

Under that is the Pauli exclusion principle, from Wolfgang Pauli in 1925: no two electrons can share the same quantum state, so atoms resist being squeezed. In the late 1960s Freeman Dyson and Andrew Lenard proved this is why ordinary matter is stable and takes up room.

thread.title: How do we know atoms are real? (7 cards)

title: Feynman's one-sentence rescue plan
text: If all science were wiped out and one sentence could survive, Richard Feynman would keep this: everything is made of atoms, tiny bits always moving.
author: Richard Feynman
source: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. I, ch. 1, Atoms in Motion (1963)
more:
His full sentence adds that atoms pull on each other when a little apart and push back when squeezed together. With a bit of imagination, he said, that one idea explains a huge amount, like why water evaporates and what temperature really is.

It also sums up this thread. Democritus guessed it, Dalton used it for chemistry, Brown saw its effects, Einstein and Perrin measured it, and Rutherford found the empty inside held firm by quantum rules.

thread.title: How do we know atoms are real? (7 cards)

text: …there is no more open door by which you can enter into the study of natural philosophy, than by considering the physical phenomena of a candle.
em: the physical phenomena of a candle
author: Michael Faraday
source: The Chemical History of a Candle, Lecture I (1861)
more:
Faraday gave these talks as a course of six lectures for a young audience at the Royal Institution in London, and they were published in 1861. With little more than candles, he showed wax melting into a cup, climbing the wick, turning to vapour and burning into water and carbon dioxide.

Faraday had little formal schooling. He started out as a bookbinder's apprentice, which may be why he was so sure anyone could learn to look at the world this way.

text: …a collection of facts is no more a science than a heap of stones is a house.
author: Henri Poincaré
source: Science and Hypothesis, ch. 9, in The Foundations of Science (Halsted trans., 1913)
more:
Henri Poincaré was one of the great mathematicians and physicists of his time, and he thought hard about what scientists actually do. The line before this one says science is built up with facts, as a house is with stones.

His point is that data alone explains nothing. A pile of measurements becomes science when someone finds the pattern that ties it together. Right after this line he adds that, above all, the scientist must foresee.

text: To doubt everything and to believe everything are two equally convenient solutions; each saves us from thinking.
author: Henri Poincaré
source: Science and Hypothesis, Introduction, in The Foundations of Science (Halsted trans., 1913)
more:
Poincaré wrote this in the introduction to Science and Hypothesis, first published in French in 1902. He was pushing back on two lazy habits. One treats every scientific claim as settled truth. The other waves the whole thing off as arbitrary guesswork.

He wanted readers to sort hypotheses instead. Which ones are necessary, which are handy conventions, and which can be checked by experiment?

text: The scientist does not study nature because it is useful; he studies it because he delights in it, and he delights in it because it is beautiful.
author: Henri Poincaré
source: Science and Method, Book I, ch. 1, in The Foundations of Science (Halsted trans., 1913)
more:
Science and Method came out in French in 1908. In this chapter, The Choice of Facts, Poincaré asks how scientists pick what to study when there are endless facts available. His answer, surprising from a hard-headed mathematician, is a sense of beauty.

He means something deeper than colours and surfaces: the harmonious order of the parts. Simple laws that tie many facts together tend to be both beautiful and useful.

text: Science is, I believe, nothing but trained and organized common sense, differing from the latter only as a veteran may differ from a raw recruit
author: Thomas Henry Huxley
source: On the Educational Value of the Natural History Sciences (1854), in Lay Sermons, Addresses and Reviews (1870)
more:
Thomas Henry Huxley, later famous as Darwin's fiercest public defender, gave this talk in 1854 to argue that science belonged in ordinary education. In his view it used the same reasoning everyone uses daily, sharpened by practice and checked more carefully.

So the habits behind it, like noticing, comparing, testing a guess and changing your mind, are open to anyone. The veteran and the recruit have the same kind of brain. One of them has had more training.

title: Earth measured with a shadow
text: On the solstice the noon Sun shone straight down a well at Syene. Alexandria's rods cast a 7.2 degree shadow. So Eratosthenes multiplied the distance by 50.
source: Wikipedia: Eratosthenes
more:
This was in the 3rd century BC. 7.2 degrees is one fiftieth of a circle. The Sun is so far away that its rays arrive almost parallel, so on a flat Earth both cities would see the same shadow. The difference shows how much the ground curves between them.

He got around 250,000 stadia. Nobody knows exactly how long his stadion was, but by many estimates he came close to the real 40,000 kilometres. His own book is lost. We know the method through a later writer, Cleomedes.

title: An element found on the Sun
text: During a solar eclipse in 1868, astronomers saw a yellow line in sunlight that matched no known element. Norman Lockyer named it helium, after the Greek for Sun.
source: Wikipedia: Helium
more:
Every element gives off light at its own set of colours, like a barcode. Spread sunlight into a spectrum and those barcodes show up as sharp lines. The new yellow line sat close to two sodium lines, so at first people assumed it was sodium.

Nobody found helium on Earth until 1895, when William Ramsay got it from gas released by a uranium mineral. It's rare here, but it's the second most abundant element in the universe, after hydrogen.

title: Marie Curie's two different Nobels
text: Marie Curie won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903 and in Chemistry in 1911. Nobody else has won Nobels in two different sciences.
source: Wikipedia: Marie Curie
more:
She was also the first woman to win a Nobel at all. The 1903 prize, shared with her husband Pierre and with Henri Becquerel, was for research on radioactivity, a word she coined. The 1911 prize was hers alone, for discovering polonium and radium. She named polonium after Poland.

Her papers are still radioactive and kept in lead-lined boxes. She died in 1934 of aplastic anaemia, very likely from years of radiation exposure.

title: Metal that melts in your hand
text: Gallium is a silvery metal that melts at about 29.76 °C, below body temperature. Hold a piece and it slumps into a shiny puddle in your palm.
source: Wikipedia: Gallium
more:
Gallium is one of four metals that are liquid at or near room temperature, along with mercury, caesium and rubidium.

In 1871 Dmitri Mendeleev left a gap in his periodic table for an unknown element he called eka-aluminium, and predicted its properties. Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran found gallium in 1875. Mendeleev had predicted a density of about 5.9 grams per cubic centimetre. The measured value is 5.904.

title: Old church windows aren't melting
text: Old church windows are said to be thicker at the bottom because glass flows. One study found medieval glass flows at most a nanometre in a billion years.
em: a nanometre in a billion years
source: Wikipedia: Glass (Reputed flow)
more:
The lumps were there from the start. Older ways of making flat glass gave ripples and uneven thickness, and smooth float glass only became common in the 1960s.

Glass is an amorphous solid. Its atoms are jumbled like a liquid's but locked in place like a solid's. A 2017 study looked at glass from Westminster Abbey dating to 1268. Even over the age of the universe, any flow at room temperature would be too small to see.

title: Why lakes freeze from the top
text: Most things shrink when they freeze. Water expands by about 9 percent, so ice floats. Lakes freeze top down, and fish get through winter in the water below.
source: Wikipedia: Ice
more:
The cause is hydrogen bonding. In liquid water, molecules tumble past each other and pack fairly close. When water freezes, each molecule locks into an open hexagonal lattice that takes up more room. Ice has a density of about 0.917 grams per cubic centimetre, against roughly 1 for liquid water.

Floating ice insulates the water under it, so lakes rarely freeze solid. Water freezing in cracks also splits rocks. Gallium expands when it solidifies too.

title: Good theories stick their necks out
text: Karl Popper said a theory is scientific if it forbids something, making a risky prediction that could turn out wrong. If nothing could ever refute it, it isn't science.
author: Karl Popper
source: The Logic of Scientific Discovery (1934)
more:
Popper noticed a contrast. Einstein's general relativity said exactly how much starlight should bend near the Sun, and the 1919 eclipse could have proved it wrong. Some popular theories of his day seemed able to explain any result at all, which Popper saw as a weakness.

The criterion is called falsifiability. Philosophers still argue about it, and real science is messier than any single rule. As a rough check it still works well.

title: Can a tiny demon beat physics?
text: Maxwell's demon minds a door between two gas boxes. It lets fast molecules through one way, slow ones the other. One side heats up for free. Who pays?
em: One side heats up for free
source: Wikipedia: Maxwell's demon
more:
The demon's memory pays. James Clerk Maxwell posed the puzzle in 1867 to show the second law of thermodynamics is statistical, and it bugged physicists for a century.

To sort molecules, the demon has to measure them and remember the results. In 1929 Leo Szilard linked measurement to entropy. Later, Rolf Landauer and Charles Bennett showed the unavoidable cost is wiping the demon's memory to make room. Erasing information always gives off heat, enough to cancel the gain.
